props.title: 24 Hour Party People
props.initialSlug: Factory Records' wild ride through Manchester music
props.initialStreaming: fuboTV, MGM+ Amazon Channel, MGM Plus Roku Premium Channel

sections.content: 24 Hour Party People captures Manchester's explosive music scene through Tony Wilson's wild ride from TV presenter to Factory Records founder. Michael Winterbottom's fourth-wall-breaking style perfectly matches the chaos and creativity of the era. Like Control (2007) and Velvet Goldmine (1998), it ditches traditional biopic formulas for something more experimental. Steve Coogan's Wilson directly addresses viewers, mixing real footage with recreations, creating a postmodern portrait of the punk and acid house movements that transformed British music.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in showing how Manchester's grimy industrial landscape birthed both punk and rave culture. From the Sex Pistols' legendary 1976 Lesser Free Trade Hall gig (attended by about 40 people who all started bands) to the Haçienda's sweaty dance floors, Winterbottom captures lightning in a bottle. Like This Is England (2006) and Human Traffic (1999), it shows how music movements grow from specific places and times, creating cultural revolutions.

Factory Records' story mirrors other legendary indie labels like Creation Records (captured in Upside Down (2010)) and 2 Tone. The film shows Wilson signing contracts in his own blood, losing money on every copy of New Order's "Blue Monday," and watching the Haçienda hemorrhage cash while changing club culture forever. It's both a celebration and cautionary tale about putting art before profit. SUBHEAD: The Manchester Sound and Beyond

sections.content: The film's portrayal of Joy Division's transition into New Order after Ian Curtis's death shows how tragedy can spark reinvention. 24 Hour Party People connects punk's raw energy to acid house's electronic revolution, with Happy Mondays bridging the gap. Like Beats (2019) and Party Monster (2003), it captures the ecstatic highs and devastating lows of club culture's golden age.
